utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. I was told that there are some preliminary matters from the parties, and the Chamber will have an issue to raise with the parties as well. I will hear from you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I wanted to raise a scheduling issue in connection with the next witness. The upcoming witness is, I don't think there's any dispute, an extraordinary international civil servant whose most recent service has been running the relief operation in Haiti for a matter of months. Indeed, he comes to the Tribunal directly from there. It's extremely important to the witness that he be able to depart The Hague on Tuesday. And I would note, in that regard, that this upcoming weekend, for example, will represent his second consecutive weekend in The Hague, in part, to accommodate the Defence request to interview him this past Monday. Now, in that regard, and in an effort to ensure that the witness is in a position to depart by Tuesday, the Prosecution has reduced its time for examination-in-chief so that the cross-examination can commence today. That would, of course, leave Friday -- a portion of today, Friday, Monday, and at least a good portion of Tuesday, to my judgement would be sufficient. But because the Wednesday would not be possible if he were to depart on Tuesday, I would also ask the Court to seriously consider and please schedule an afternoon hearing for tomorrow or Monday. We've checked the courtroom schedules. They're both available. I think that would ensure, to the maximum extent possible, that this witness, who's already devoted an extraordinary amount of his time, time which is demanded by many people, the effort to bring his evidence before the Tribunal. And I would also add that this would not result in an unexpected cross-examination by the accused on Wednesday of an accelerated witness. We wouldn't be bringing a witness forward for that purpose. So the accused would not be facing the cross-examination of a witness before he anticipated that. So under these circumstances, Your Honours, I would please ask the Court to determine whether, indeed, those courtrooms are available - I believe they are - and to schedule an afternoon session for either Friday or Monday for this purpose. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So to be clear, there will be no sitting on Wednesday next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Under the -- yeah, under these circumstances, that's precisely what I would ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Robinson, do you have any say to this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this certainly doesn't work to the benefit of the Defence. If the witness has the ambition to present not only his knowledge, but also his beliefs and feelings, and we did discuss that because he was kind enough to come to see me, anyway, this doesn't work in favour of the Defence. As for the quantity of material that the Prosecution wants to tender through this witness, that will not be reduced; on the contrary. However, we'll do our best. I would like to avail myself of this opportunity to express a certain concern, since I've already had some negative experience. It's not only that this system is totally unknown to us, but even within that system, it seems to me that the Prosecution and witnesses can do whatever they want to do and say whatever they want to say, and the Defence has to state that or to refute their lies. I understand that a witness doesn't have to know anything about a particular document, but the document speaks of something that is quite different to what, say, this particular witness now is saying. It is the very opposite. So if lopsided statements are being admitted into evidence, I have to challenge the witness by saying that the documents of her government, or of various intelligence services, showed that that was not the case, that the phenomenon, itself, was different. That's why I'm asking for a certain degree of understanding. We want to show what is not true, and that is what an investigative judge would do within our system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Back to the scheduling issue regarding the next witness. So due to these circumstances of the Chamber, it not being possible to sit the whole day tomorrow, but a certain extension would be possible, though, we'll try to sit the whole day -- we'll sort out the way in which we will be sitting on Monday, and then we'll be sitting in the morning of Tuesday, and in that way we'll try to accommodate the situations triggered by the witness's circumstances. Shall we go back to private session briefly -- go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we finish up the cross-examination of Ms. Zaimovic, I would like to clarify the Chamber's position with regard to some of the documents put to her yesterday by Mr. Karadzic. The Chamber has had the opportunity to re-read the transcript of yesterday's hearing, and has given further thought to the admission of certain documents. In light of this further consideration, we are going to reverse our decision on the admission of certain documents and give some guidance on the practice that we expect both parties to follow in the future. I recall the comments made by my colleague His Honour Judge Morrison yesterday afternoon concerning questioning of witnesses about documents which they have no knowledge of or cannot speak to. The Chamber is of the view that, in these circumstances, such documents should not be admitted into evidence, even where there is no dispute about authenticity or even relevance. In addition to relevance and authenticity, the Chamber must be satisfied as to the probative value of a piece of proposed evidence, and this requires that the witness to whom it is shown is able to confirm its content or make some other positive comment about it. We take Mr. Tieger's point that to do otherwise is essentially the same as admitting the document from the Bar table. While there may be circumstances in which such admission from the Bar table is appropriate, the Chamber has already issued a decision stating that this should be the exception rather than the rule, and stringent requirements have to be met before a document will be accepted into evidence from the Bar table. For these reasons, the Chamber has reconsidered its decision to admit documents 1D902, now marked as Exhibit D122, and 1D905, which is now admitted as D121, and instructs the Registry, the Court Officer, to now mark these documents as not admitted. Similarly, we marked for identification a number of documents yesterday pending English translation. Even once the English translation of these documents are available, the Chamber will not admit them into evidence on the same basis; namely, the witness was unable to confirm them or comment on their content. There is, therefore, no reason for them to remain marked for identification, and the Registry Court Officer should remove these designations from them. The documents in question are: 1D903, MFI Exhibit D124; 1D920, MFI Exhibit D126; 1D946, MFI 1D27; 1D949, MFI Exhibit 128; 1D950, MFI Exhibit D129. The Chamber advises both parties to only tender for admission into evidence a document put to a witness either on direct or on cross-examination which the witness has been able to speak to. This does not prevent you, Mr. Karadzic, from putting any document you wish to a witness. But if the witness is clearly unable to say anything about the document, it will not be admitted and you should not keep putting questions to the witness about it. What I would like to add to this is that this rule will apply evenly to the Prosecution when they will be cross-examining the Defence witnesses during the course of the Defence case. Otherwise, the Chamber will be inundated with a lot of Prosecution documents. That said, we'll continue with Mr. Karadzic's cross-examination. And I urge you to try to finish your cross-examination as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, just while the witness is coming in, I would like to just make two observations about the Chamber's ruling. First of all, I think we also have to revisit the admission of 92 ter-associated exhibits, because you'll see that there are contained in those exhibits documents that the witness could not really speak to, but that were emphasising points that the witness had made during their testimony; for example, Ambassador Okun had -- there was admitted shorthand notes from the session of the Council for Co-ordinating Positions on the state Policy that he never attended or knew nothing about. We had the same vision that the Prosecution had about the admission of documents, and we didn't object to the 92-ter-associated exhibits at the time. But if we're going to change the rules and require that the witness have a knowledge of the document, then it seems like we also should revisit the admission of documents already with previous witnesses when we've had a different point of view. That's one point. And my second point is that I still think it's necessary -- well, it's advisable that documents be marked for identification even if they're not -- don't meet your standards of admissibility, because in the Defence case, should we try to admit those documents or discuss them, it's -- in order to keep track of which document was shown to the witness, I think there ought to be some designation of that document that was shown to the witness, and usually marking for identification is the way that that designation is done. So I would ask that you continue to allow the documents to be marked for identification, and then later on we'll have a way to link those documents to the witness that testified about them, even though they weren't admitted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before Judge Morrison responds to you, there are two procedural matters. The Chamber has decided not to revisit all the previous exhibits that have been admitted, so we limited our reconsideration to those that took place yesterday. And as for the MFI'ing -- marking for identification practice, it causes a lot of administrative problems in keeping, maintaining, monitoring, those things. We are using the e-court system, and then we have the 65 ter number in the transcript, so all the Defence evidence can be traceable through transcript, through e-court, so I don't think MFI'ing things are absolutely necessary. Judge Morrison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, you said the witness had a knowledge of the document, and that's not, strictly speaking, necessary, that the witness have a knowledge of the document. If the document is used as an aide-memoire or a source for cross-examination, and the witness positively responds by agreeing to a question that is put, or accepting a factual matter contained in the document, then the document can be exhibited. So they don't have to have prior knowledge of the document. They simply have to adopt it in some meaningful evidential way. I reiterate what the President has said about the 65 ter numbers. That should be an adequate way of dealing with the -- I appreciate your position on that. It could otherwise become unmanageable. But the reason to repeat that which the President said is this: that this is really for the benefit not simply of the Chamber, but of both parties. If we get to a stage where Dr. Karadzic has hundreds or even thousands of documents put to him by the Prosecution with which he does not agree or his witnesses do not agree, there is no logical reason why those should go into evidence, any more the Defence documents. This is a balancing exercise for the benefit of all parties, so that the only things which are exhibited as evidence truly merit evidential consideration. Of course, there is nothing to prevent a document which is not exhibited ab initio through a witness from becoming an exhibit because it is spoken to by secondary evidence during the course, for instance, of the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Welcome back, Ms. Zaimovic. I hope you had a good rest yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Ms. Zaimovic.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to go back to a few things that you said, things that you described in quite a bit of detail, but without any proof, or, rather, there was a lack of precision involved. Before that, I would like to ask the usher to show a certain name to you. Please don't read it out, so that we don't have to go into closed session. I'm just going to ask you whether you know that person. Could somebody help me, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Show it to the Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ms. Zaimovic, do you know that person?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't. Judging by the last name and the first name -- no, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. How come you sent that person to be disciplined? This person was sent to a commission because she wrote that she was -- this person wrote that he or she was an ethnic Serb and of Orthodox religion.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not send anyone to a disciplining commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You did not? And Dr. Andrija Gvozdenovic intervened, stating that this kind of discrimination and mistreatment should stop, because this person had declared herself or himself as an Orthodox Serb; you're saying you didn't do that?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't, and that is certainly true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are going to obtain proof.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I don't know this name at all, and I know all of my nurses or all the doctors who worked with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: She did not work with you as a nurse?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, she did not. I don't know her.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that you are a caring person, you care about other people's children, and you certainly care about your own as well. Did you go to visit your son at the front-line?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did Islam go?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then your son came home; right?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from time to time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How often?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, say once a month, or twice a month, in order to take a bath.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where were his positions?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I've already told you that. I know that he was in Azici for a while, down there, and that's the only thing I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At one point, did 150 wounded persons come to your hospital from Azici?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Azici, indeed, a lot of people were brought to the state hospital down there, and probably to our hospital as well. But since I worked at the children's surgical ward, I did not see these wounded men.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that you didn't talk to your son about anything in relation to the war, the conflict, the deaths, the shellings; nothing?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I talked to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, are you going to share some of that with us?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that really matters. It's not really important for this Court to hear what I discussed with my son. I didn't come here to talk about that. I came to say something completely different. I came to speak about children who were victims during the war, and I would like to ask you to allow me to speak of the children who lost their arms, their legs, who suffered so greatly during the war. Perhaps you're going to recognise some of the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ms. Zaimovic, with all due respect, in addition to the names of these children and their suffering, you said a great many other things as well that I have to challenge and deny in various ways. Are you denying that Muslim soldiers sometimes used shells and sometimes sniper fire to kill people in Sarajevo, including children?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that did not happen, because their dignity would not allow them to do that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that Musan Topalovic, Caco; Ramiz Delalic, Celo; the other Celo as well, Juka Prazina, and all these notorious criminals, had a dignity that prevented them from committing crimes against their own people?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see how you can twist things that way. They defended the city, though. What kind of people they were, I don't know. I just heard that they defended the city. And I doubt that they committed these crimes. You are twisting the facts without providing any arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if I put it to you, Ms. Zaimovic, that French soldiers and other soldiers of the UN established that your soldiers were killing your own children with sniper fire, that they even saw a girl who fell victim to sniper fire and probably ended up in your hospital, are you saying that the United Nations also lie?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be the judge of that, but I don't think that what you are saying is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ms. Zaimovic, I'm trying not to share with you what I know, but what the United Nations know and what your government knows. I would like to call up 1D941. This is a report issued by your Ministry of the Interior of the Sarajevo Security Services Centre, which was sent to everybody, the 1st Corps of the BiH Army, the Staff of the Supreme Command, to the MUP, to the under-secretary for state security, and so on and so forth. And we will see the document, in which it says information about some activities in the base of the 2nd Independent Battalion of the BiH Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the translation which is in e-court is not the translation of the B/C/S document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that there is a translation, however.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we'll try only with the B/C/S version. I was told that there's no matching English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ms. Zaimovic, this is a document issued by your Ministry of the Interior, which also includes State Security. It says here in this document that the Independent Battalion of the BiH Army, in Mosa Pijade Street, to be more precise, on the ground floor, the commander of the unit is Adnan Solakovic, and lately the commander of the 10th Mountain Brigade, Musan Topalovic, departed, Caco, has been visiting the headquarters more frequently. Did you know of him?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that he was killed in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the police turned against Caco only when he killed the son of Avdo Hebib, the minister of the police?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that that's not correct. However, you should ask the MUP as to how that transpired. But I don't think it's the way you are describing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I received information from Bosnia that they had lost everything, that everything had gone missing, and that we can't get hold of anything. We'll have to try to talk to the Trial Chamber to make them provide us with anything. You see how Solakovic privately established a crossroads at the entrance of Mesa Selimovic Road, and myofascial surgery, there is a barricade of three sandbags, and it says on the upper floor of the hospital there's also a bunker which controls the entire plateau of transfixiology [as interpreted] and most of Nemanjina Street, as well as the crossroads of the aforementioned street with Mosa Pijade Street. Do you see that Bolnicka used to be Mosa Pijade Street?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. On reflection, I realise that you're right, that it used to be called Mosa Pijade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In front of the bunker, there is a concrete plate, 30 by 10 metres large, where four vehicles are parked, two of them ambulances, and also an APC. That APC is very interesting, because it is the sentry point for a guard who is standing there with a death sower. On the third floor of the stomatology surgery, there are two or three sniper nests which are distributed in such a way as to cover the plateau of the gas station in Kosevo. And the following sentence -- and most of the Mosa Pijade Street and the area around the School of Medicine. And the following sentence: "In all these sentry points, there are mostly two men deployed in full combat gear. At the very entrance into the hospital, we noticed guards in blue flak-jackets, and we realised -- we learned from some sources that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, are you reading out something?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether the witness is following.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm already on page 3. I'm already on page 3. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go back to page 2. You will see the beginning of what I was reading. I apologise. I was not following what was on the screen. Can we have the second page of the document, please. I just read out what Adnan Solakovic was doing, and can this please be enlarged. And Musan Topalovic, also known as Caca, and here, I described how he created a special zone in the middle of this city which he reinforced in order to be completely safe from the police and to be completely autonomous. Now we can go to page 3, please. Page 3, please. Yes, thank you. "On the third floor --" If you look at the third line from the top of the page: "On the third floor of the stomatology ward, there are temporarily two or three sniper nests which are distributed in such a way as to cover the plateau in front of the Kosevo gas station."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ms. Zaimovic, do you know what the sniper range is?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. Mr. Karadzic, I have never held a pistol or any other kind of weaponry in my hands, nothing that one could shoot from. But now I'm asking you, what kind of secret documents are these, who wrote them? Were they written by your people? Is this war propaganda? What am I supposed to do with this? I don't have a clue what this is. I apologise. This is something that I never saw. I don't know who made bunkers, who did this or that. What was done in the city, I really don't know. My job for four years was to go from my house to my hospital. I rarely went into town. I was afraid of shelling and sniper fire and everything else. And that was my range, that's what I did. I went to work and back home, and very often I did that under sniper fire and bullets. It never occurred to me to go to another part of the city, let alone try to see where sniper nests are. This was probably done by your own people, who were probably spies in our own units. This is a military matter. I'm not here to deal with any military matters. You have to understand that. Ask me something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ms. Zaimovic, this was not done by my men. This was signed by Munir Alibabic, a high official and the chief in the Security Services Centre in Sarajevo; a Muslim, as you know. And these are documents issued by the Muslim government in the middle of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why don't you ask him when he comes here?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Madam, you say that we were the ones who targeted targets.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You did, you climbed Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the bunker between the School of Stomatology and myofascial surgical ward, is that a civilian target?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So how are you -- why are you saying that we targeted civilian targets?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You targeted everything; houses, hospitals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I know that you're not aware of the sniper range.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know any ranges. I don't know what the shell range is. I don't know what a sniper range is. I've never held a pistol or any other piece of weaponry in my hands, nothing that could kill people. That's far removed from me. That's how I was brought up; kindly. Please, do not talk to me about these things. This is a military matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Madam, I apologise. Just for the transcript, I would like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: You need to slow down a bit. Because you're entering into what is, in effect, argument, rather than cross-examination, which is not the way you should be proceeding, in any event, you're both speaking - both you and the witness - are speaking very fast, and I don't know how the interpreters are keeping up with it. They are, just, but it must be exceptionally wearing for them, and it's very difficult for the Trial Chamber to follow it. So can you please slow it down sufficiently to allow the interpreters to do a proper job.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Accepted. Just for the transcript, I apologise to the interpreters. The witness said that that was not a civilian target, and in the transcript it says that it was a civilian target.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that correct; did you say that you understand that those bunkers were not civilian targets? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you just say that you passed under sniper fire and through bullets?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the rifle range is?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Will you accept if I told you that the range of an automatic rifle is less than a kilometre; of a sniper, a kilometre and a half at the most; and that the Serbian positions were never any closer than two to three kilometres from the area that you just described?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you want me to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Whose bullets were those, if you had to pass through a torrent of bullets in the area where the Serb rifles couldn't reach? And you see that there were snipers and there are bunkers in the middle of the town, and they were not turned towards the Serbs, but towards the citizens of Sarajevo; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were huge bullets, big bullets. I don't know what they're called. They zoomed by. They pierced the walls. That's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're talking about rifle bullets, and now you're mentioning 12.7. You are the ones who had it, your army had those from the very beginning, and we only had them towards the end of the war. But, in any case, even such a sniper range is not more than two and a half kilometres. But I'm describing something that everybody could see in the street, bunkers in the middle of the town, and those bunkers were not turned towards the Serbs, Serb positions. They were made in order to secure the gang from either the citizens or the police, and the police reported to the authorities that in the centre of the town there was a bunker which was not within their control, there were sniper nests, there were APCs, and, madam, that was in the street. It was in Bolnicka Street or, rather, Mosa Pijade Street. How come -- how is it possible that you didn't see that?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I didn't, and it is crazy -- it would have been crazy for people living in town to open fire on their own people. That's your fabrication. I really don't understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, it may be a crazy idea, but it's not my idea. Madam, this is a Muslim document. Can we go back to the previous page, to page 1. Do you deny -- I apologise. On page 3, it says: "Members of the aforementioned units are bragging that they have 15 machine-guns, death sower, they have nitroglycerine rifles, and so on and so forth. In other words, your police is here reporting us to what was going on in a neighbourhood, and Serb rifles could not reach those positions because that was about more than three kilometres away from the Serb lines; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I know nothing about all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Madam, you say that the entrance into the hospital, you were shot at from a sniper; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who was it who could open fire at you, since the Serbs were more than two and a half kilometres away from that place? Who could it have been that opened fire on you?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You armed all your Serbs in Sarajevo, and you gave all of them weapons. You know that. I suppose that somebody opened fire from their own window, and you know that also. I don't know where, from, and how.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that there were Serb units in Sarajevo, within Sarajevo, which was under the control of the Muslim Army, the Muslim police, and Muslim criminals: Caco, Solakovic, Juka Prazina. And terror was targeted at Serbs only because they were Serbs, just like your nurse who had to present herself to the disciplinary commission only because she declared herself as an Orthodox Serb?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that person at all, and I never sent any of the nurses to present themselves to the disciplinary commission because I dealt with those matters myself. You know that and you can see it in all the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I'm want to be clear I'm not trying to curtail or limit the accused's cross-examination in any way. However, I wonder how many times he would be permitted to ask essentially the same question which has already been answered by the witness, who explained the limits of her knowledge about military matters, on the basis of a document she knows little about, and formulated in the form of lengthy argument, with compound propositions presented to the witness, and then asking the witness essentially to comment on things she's already said she's not in a position to provide information on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I took it he was wrapping up his cross-examination. Bear that in mind, what Mr. Tieger has said, and then just be brief in your questioning. Let's conclude your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot bring my cross-examination to an end in that way. There are a lot of matters that either have to be confirmed or refuted. And these are documents. Can I tender this document into evidence, because this document was produced by the Ministry of the Interior of the Muslim government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We object to the admission of this document, pursuant to the directions that Your Honours gave earlier this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, that is obviously contingent upon whether or not the document is an agreed document. If the document is agreed, as between the Prosecution and Defence, as being an accurate document, then it falls to be an agreed document and it can be exhibited, exactly the same way as a Prosecution document could be. It really turns upon whether or not the contents of the document are agreed or disputed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry. I apologise to Your Honour and to Ms. Sutherland, but I just want to make a distinction, before any response is made, between the provenance of the document, that is, it is a document that was produced by that particular authority, and the accuracy of the contents of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, yes, plainly if a document is -- if it is agreed that the provenance is accurate, and it is, in fact, as it were, a true document - whether it is an original or exact copy perhaps doesn't matter - then the distinction then becomes whether or not the contents are true. Well, that's something that can be later disputed. But if you are not disputing that this document is, in fact, an accurate representation of a government document, and the fact that this witness has agreed to certain matters in it, then it may tend towards it being exhibited. But if you take the view -- if you dispute the provenance of that document, that would be different.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. I thought I was -- I wanted to make a clarification, but I think I muddled it slightly. In any event, I think this is not a document which we dispute the provenance of. However, as with many of these documents, Ms. Sutherland may have a different position, but I think we're seeing many of them for the first time. So I -- if you want to mark that for identification, we can have that checked. I don't think -- I think this is a document that falls within the category you just alluded to, Your Honour, and that it will be admitted, but -- and perhaps I should never have arisen. Perhaps I should have allowed Ms. Sutherland to, because -- Oh, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, in any event, as we know, this is a document that has not been translated, so it would have to be MFI'd in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Once a document is tendered into evidence and exhibited, unless otherwise specifically directed, it is admitted for all purposes, including for the truth of its content. So bearing that in mind, we will rather stick to our rule we set out at the beginning of today's hearing, and then the witness didn't confirm anything about the content of the document. And, Mr. Karadzic, you will have another opportunity to introduce this exhibit, so we will not admit it. Let's proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. But, again, I'd like to ask to be given enough time for my cross-examination. This way, I simply cannot do all the things I want to do. I want to deal with the shortest possible parts of documents that I have on my list. D909 now, please. I asked for six hours, and you're not even giving me four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I think you misunderstood that which the learned President said. He wasn't suggesting you would curtail your cross-examination immediately; simply as far as this document was concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Try to conclude your examination -- cross-examination by this session, and then we will see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ms. Zaimovic, do you know this person, Ramiz Delalic, Celo?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about him, but I've never seen him. I've never seen him in real life.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you see him on TV?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't seem to remember. I have to tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that he killed a member of a wedding party on the 1st of March, 1992, because he carried a Serb flag during a wedding, in front of the old church at Bascarsija?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was carried by the newspapers and the television. I know about it from the media, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that when the war started, he went on TV and he boasted of this heroic deed?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted into evidence, because the content has been confirmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, she did not recognise this picture.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But this man was treated at their ward. 1D938.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ms. Zaimovic, while we're waiting for that: Again, it's the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Ministry of Defence, the Security Department, that is to say, the authorities in the Muslims part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. What we have here is a bulletin. We probably saw it a moment ago. I think that there is a translation. Isn't that right? Now let us look at page 3 of this document. Could I please have page 3? This is 1. I need page 3. It says here: "According to information of the Security Service of the 1st Corps, on the 21st of April, 1994, the former commander of this brigade, Zakir Puskar, and the former deputy commander of the brigade, Babic, Sead, visited the Command of the 2nd Brigade and had a heated discussion in relation to the alleged release of Ramiz Delalic, Celo. Delalic is currently being treated at the Kosevo Hospital and has submitted a request to be transferred to the eye department because of his eye problems." That ward shares the same entrance with you; right?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not exactly the same entrance, but it's the same building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that Ramiz Delalic, Celo, was being treated in your building?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about that, because I was treating children.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you notice a security detail, because when these people are being treated, there has to be security there?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was always security there at the front desk. You know that. That's the way it is to this day. It was that way before the war, during the war. The very entrance at the front desk, there were always people who were providing security for the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I meant the security detail from his unit. Who was chief of security for the entire hospital; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot remember who the chief of security was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you did remember that you heard of Amir Huskic, Kinez; right?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard the name, but I never met him personally and I don't know who he is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You don't want to admit this document either, do you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ms. Zaimovic, have you heard of Dr. Sinisa Markovic?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't even know where he worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He was a surgeon employed at the Clinic of Plastic Surgery. Does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I have heard of him. I don't know. He must belong to a younger generation, so I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D912, please. Could I have that document now. 1D912.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What we see here in the first section, he's a surgeon employed at the Clinic of Plastic Surgery. Now let us go on to page 2. There are a few other relevant things here as well, but let's move on to page 2. It says here: "In the previous period --"

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can we have the translation up in e-court, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note that there's none.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There doesn't seem to be one. I'll read it out slowly. So this has to do with Dr. Sinisa Markovic. This is a conversation with Sinisa Markovic. He was at this clinic that was headed by Professor Dr. Starovic, and it says here: "Celo blocked the center of town. There were conflicts ..." Et cetera. However, what is important on this page 2 is as follows: "In this previous period in front of the clinical centre, there was a T-55 tank that opened fire at Serb positions in Poljine, and that was registered by members of UNPROFOR. Later on, the tank was moved to a different location. Also, a tank targeted Vogosca from the area of Ciglana, and after a few precise hits, the very entrance of the tunnel by the Serb soldiers, it stopped operating."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that you marked the entrance to the tunnel near the hospital?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I marked it because that's what you asked me to do. You asked me to mark it, and I marked it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that in that tunnel, in one part there was a prison where Serbs were held, and in another part there were at least two tanks that went out from time to time, fired, and then went back? Did you know about this tank that was in front of the clinical centre where you worked?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I don't know about any of that. All of these things that you are asking me about now is Greek to me, as people would say. I would really want you to ask me about children, wounded children, and about the situation at the ward. If you looked into the eyes of a mother losing her child. Have you ever looked at a mother who was in that position? Have you ever seen her eyes if she was losing child and then yet another child? That is what I have been saying all along. That's why I came here. That's what I came here to talk about. I don't know about any of this, for heaven's sake, all of this you're showing me now. I never did anything to harm a single person ever in my life. I was always trying to help patients. That's why I worked. You left medicine a long time ago. You are not a physician any longer. I, however, have remained a nurse, and I'm proud of that because I helped people all my life. I helped wounded people, regardless of what their names were. That is what I want you to ask me about, please. I do apologise for speaking about all of this, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: May I intervene here. We fully appreciate how you feel. We really do. But, you see, Dr. Karadzic is exercising a right, an entitlement, to ask you questions. Now, he is self-represented. If he were represented, then his attorney would have asked you the questions. But he is self-represented, so he is asking the questions. Now, they might appear to be difficult for you, they might appear to be not relevant for you, but the point is: Until such time that they have been objected to, and the objection is sustained, then answer the questions as best you can. We do appreciate how you feel, but this is the procedure, and Dr. Karadzic is actually following it. But please. Yes, Dr. Karadzic, carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ms. Zaimovic, I'm asking you about things that are so obvious, like a tank and other such things. Let me ask you something else now. You said that you saw a Serb tank by Osmice. Can we have that map again, the one that was shown by the Prosecution? Yes, it was the Prosecutor that showed that map, with lines that are marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is he referring to the first page of this binder?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. The number is 0546-6574.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's P815.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have it in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ms. Zaimovic, can you indicate where it was that you saw a tank? Can you see where Osmice is, actually?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot. I'm not very knowledgeable about maps, but you know where Osmice is. That's a restaurant that you destroyed as soon as the war started, and there is that big rock right next to it. You know that full well. And behind that rock, that's where the tank hid, and it's only 50 metres away from my terrace, as the crow flies. You know Breka very well as well. I could, indeed, see a tank getting out from behind that rock and firing at town. That's what I said, and that is the way it was. But please leave me alone with these maps. I never knew about maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will say that between your house and Osmice, it's at least three kilometres, not 50 metres.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you, as the crow flies, 50 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we have the scale down here, and we can see exactly what two, three, and four kilometres is. And now look at the upper part, where it says "Centre."

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see "Kosevo"?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And to the right, do you see your own neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And opposite that neighbourhood, you have Osmice and Trebevic; right?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, look how far away that is.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it's very far away. I tell you, I sit on my terrace and I can see that, and that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ms. Zaimovic, may I draw your attention to the scale down here in the lower right-hand corner, where it says what half a kilometre is, what one, two, three, and four kilometres are. And look at the distance as the crow flies from your house and Osmice.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So what are you trying to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not trying to say anything. I'm just trying to establish what it was that you had seen.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you what I saw, and I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is Osmice opposite your house?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, opposite my terrace, my balcony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: To the south, right, but Grbavica, towards the south; right?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, since we see the scale here, we see that that is over three kilometres. Now, tell me, can you see the red-and-blue front-line?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's far away. Are you talking about this red line here?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, the red and blue lines that follow one another, as it were.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you believe that the front-lines at Trebevic were 20 to 50 metres away from each other?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. Please leave me alone with all this military business. You mastered that full well, all of this strategy and military stuff and whatever. I never knew anything about it. Please leave me alone. Whoever wants to check can come and see what it was that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Madam, you said that you saw a tank, and you even saw a shell being fired from the tank?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and the shell could be seen as it flew towards the apartment buildings there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, madam, that shell is fired at a speed of 1300 metres per second.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So how can you see that?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you can. You can see exactly how it's pulled and how it goes out, how it's fired, how the shell is fired from that barrel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Madam, I have to tell you a few things, and then you can tell us whatever you want. The distance from your house is at least three kilometres.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Okay, as the crow flies. We can see the scale here. It is impossible for the tank to stay on the Serb line if the Muslim line is only 20 to 50 metres away. That tank would have been destroyed immediately from a hand-held rocket-launcher.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was hidden behind the rock. Do you know how big the rock is?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Okay, let me just tell me you a few things that refute all that you're saying. The United Nations control the positions of the Serb weaponry, and a shell that would have exited the tank barrel could not be seen. The tank could not have been standing in that place, because it could not have targeted anything in the town. There would be a dead angle for the tank if it had been standing there. It could only be firing above your house. Therefore, madam, did you see a Serb tank or a Muslim tank? If that was 50 metres from your house, it must have been a Muslim tank.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not correct. Those were your positions up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I must tell you that it is impossible, that you saw something you didn't see, and you didn't see a tank in front of the hospital, and you did not hear it fire.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see anything in front of the hospital, and I doubt there were tanks in front of the house. And up on the hills, all your tanks were there, and you fired upon all of us down there, and you know it only too well. And it says so on all the maps, on all the papers that I saw subsequently. I saw how you surrounded Sarajevo. Not a fly could get through, and you know it only too well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could Ms. Zaimovic be provided with a pen to mark Osmice and her own neighbourhood where she resided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we do it after zooming on that map a little bit further or -- but, Ms. Zaimovic, you can locate the place you are living in -- how do you pronounce, the Osmice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't find Osmice. I was close to the centre across the street from the hospital, and that would be somewhere here [indicates]. I don't know if I can read this map well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Above the hospital compound, to the right, to the right, where you were just a minute ago. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here [indicates] is about where you would say, this is where I was. I really cannot read maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now from there straight to the south, that's where Osmice is?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here [indicates]? Probably somewhere above.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, no, southwards, in the direction of Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is Trebevic on this map?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Go south. Go south towards Nova Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here [indicates], is that it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please leave me be with all that. I don't want to look at any maps. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think it would be --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want you not to show me any maps. I don't want to see any maps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My microphone was not working. I don't think it's assisting the Chamber, unless you go to there and you give testimony. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will give it a second thought a bit later. The fact is that Osmice is in the opposite direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Madam, between where you lived and Osmice, were there any walls, were there any trees? You mentioned trees, did you not?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What trees?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that you could not see anything from the hospital because of the trees.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what you're asking me now. If you're asking me about my ward and whether I could see anything from the windows of the hospital from my ward, I said no, and you know it very well. In front of our ward, in front of the pediatrics ward, there are huge chestnut trees which prevent any view to the city and to the gate, and those chestnut trees are still in the same place where they were before, on both sides of the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But that applies to others as well. The other person looking in the direction of your building could not see it, and if a shell was fired, it would have ended up in the chestnut tree branches?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what happens to shells when they're fired. I only know that they ended up in the hospital, in the wards, everywhere.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document please be removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The fact is that the distance was not 50 metres. If you had seen a tank at a 50-metre distance, then have you to accept that it was a Muslim tank.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As for the location or the distance from two places, you can prove it through other means, and you can even think about getting stipulation from the Prosecution. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could the Court please produce --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, how much longer do you have?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was hoping to have at least two more hours, one whole session. There are a lot of things that have been said here, and I have ways to demonstrate that they were not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You don't have to put everything to the witness, as I told you before. You spent about two hours and forty minutes, and after the break you will have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You will have an hour in the next session to finish your cross-examination. We have five more minutes. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ms. Zaimovic, you said that people of Serb nationality were not evicted from their apartments and that apartments were never a business proposition in Sarajevo, and that Dr. Milica Lopandic committed suicide and she was not thrown out a window; because such things happen, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of Marko Vesovic?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was a poet. The name does ring a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. And did you ever hear of Zarko Bulic, a famous lawyer?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm now going to read to you what Marko Vesovic wrote in his book in 1994. Marko Vesovic says --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter remarks that it will not be possible to interpret if Mr. Karadzic is going to read from an untranslated text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The interpreters were not able to follow your fast reading. I think we heard that poet some days ago -- yesterday. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to show you some 10 sources which say that that was a business in Sarajevo. Serbs were being thrown out of their apartments, and their apartments were then confiscated. Those Serbs were on the Muslim side, and both Muslims and Serbs confirm that that was, indeed, done. And this lady has to know about it. If she doesn't, then there's something wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not correct, as far as I know. Those things didn't happen. This must have been your propaganda. You fabricated that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is your writer, Marko Vesovic. They threw him from the fourth floor, but something incredible happened. He remained alive, but then they returned him to the fourth floor, and then they threw him away, and then he died. Ahmo had captured him three times, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe these are Marko's poetic expressions. You have to ask Marko. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of the family Nevstrujev? Djordje Nevstrujev was a prosecutor. Do you remember them?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never heard of that family.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that Marina Nevstrujev was taken from her apartment, and on the following morning somebody moved into her apartment? Obviously, Zarko Bulic concluded that that person must have known that that woman would never return.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you're asking me about things that I don't know. And you expelled thousands upon thousands of people carrying only two plastic bags in Banja Luka, in Srebrenica, and from all the other places. How are you not ashamed of asking me things like that? Thousands of Muslims and Croats you expelled, you killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Madam [Realtime transcript read in error "Madam damn"], you don't know that.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know it, I know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you have to know things that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Don't argue with the witness. I'm doubting the relevance of this line of questions. Ms. Sutherland, you wanted to raise something?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to say, Mr. Karadzic put a question to the witness: "Did you ever hear of the family Nevstrujev," sorry for my mispronunciation. The witness said: "No, I never heard of that family." But then he proceeded to say: "Do you know that she was taken from her apartment," and so forth, when the witness has clearly already said that she's never heard of the family name. So the next question is, in my respectful opinion, superfluous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I can't agree more. Mr. Karadzic, we'll have a break for 25 minutes now, and after which you should conclude your cross-examination in an hour's time. And concentrate on relevant questions. Twenty-five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to introduce your new member, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We're joined by Ms. Carolyn Edgerton, and she will be leading the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Since I have only another hour left, I would like to speed things along, and I would like to eliminate some of the documents and video materials that I wanted to show. Could I please start with 1D1000. That's a video-clip. I will have some questions for the witness about people depicted in the video-clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you have it on the screen, madam, in e-court?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Where is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know this person?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who is that?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's Professor Dr. Mirko Sosic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could the first clip be played.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no sound.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "To leave the town happened on August the 14th when I came to work, two haggard nurses told me that one of our colleagues was brought dead and massacred that night. That man was Professor Dr. Milutin Najdanovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know Professor Najdanovic?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He was a famous professor, doctor at the thoracic surgery?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And he worked with Professor Sosic, Dr. Dosendo [phoen], and others?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And he was married to the daughter of Isak Samokovlija, the great author?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Was that a good man, an imminent person in good standing as a doctor?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we continue at 33:59.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "His body was deformed. He had about 14 knife stabs. He was fired in the mouth, and he was found on the pavement in front of the Zetra during the night. And because of all that, his body was not recognisable. They called one of the paramedics who were on duty that night, and that person identified him. That was the crucial moment when I realised that nothing was left for me there, that maybe I would be the next victim."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know what had happened to Professor Najdanovic?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did you hear that he had been killed?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that he had been killed, that actually something had happened to him, but I didn't hear of the details.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please see 1D01006. Let's see how things were before the war, before the war, a few months before the war, in your hospital. 1D1006.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Yes. It was in December 1991. While I was entering the hospital, some beardless man in berets, armed with Klashnikovs, that were armed -- pointed the gun into me, and they asked me, Who are you? I said that I was a doctor and that I worked there. What are you carrying? I said that I was carrying my purse, my things. They started to search me. That was December, much before the war. It was a few months before the war. Then I came in and asked my colleagues, the doctors, what had happened over the night. I asked who it was who was terrorising the doctors. And they told me that some measures of caution had to be put in place because the well-known leader of one paramilitary unit had been wounded and put on trauma, and his forces were controlling the whole hospital, who entered, who exited. But that was much before the war, you know. And we, the doctors, we were infuriated. We decided to call the police. We called the police, the commander of the police, Bjelave, and the police told us, There's nothing we can do, and they hung up. The war actually started much before we could hear the first shots."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that you were the only one who did not see what was happening in the hospital in December 1991? That hospital was occupied; did you know? Did you see that the hospital had been occupied by his paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ER is a bit further from our ward, as you know, and in the hospital there are security people who were standing at the gate, at the entrance to the hospital. And whenever we, the staff, went through, nobody ever searched me. So what Professor Sosic is saying here, I really don't know anything about that. He was a very nice gentleman. His wife worked at my ward. She had retired before the war started. And I have to tell you, honestly, that I was very surprised when he had left our country -- our part of the town, because when doctors leave, that's very difficult. And I don't know why he left, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It is true that the ER is a bit further, but Professor Sosic said that the entire hospital was occupied, that there were paramilitaries everywhere. Can we now look at 1D1002. Do you know the person who's going to appear on the screen?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. What's his name?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Marko Vukovic. Is this Dr. Marko Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "On 2nd January, five men came to me and said, We are the police. Are you Vukovic? Yes, that's me. Open the door. One of them pointed an automatic gun at me, and the other one pointed some strong light into my eyes. The other three men entered into my house, rampaging around. They said to me, Get ready immediately. One of them approached quite incorrectly and telling me to get dressed and wear my clothes, and then they put me in the van to look for their Dr. Veljkov. He lived in Kosevsko Brdo, but he was not at home. They took Dr. Sabljak, a Croat, and they put him next to me, and then they took us both towards the hospital in Kosevo, looking for Dr. Veljkov. They didn't find him. They called Dr. Kafka in Dolac-Malta, and then the next day they brought Dr. Veljkov and a certain gynaecologist. I think his name was Mandic or something similar. He works now as a gynaecologist in Podgorica. They didn't beat us. They took us to the police station. There, we stayed over the night, the next day and the following night, and then they took us to the Central Prison, and we were sentenced. I got 28 months, Kafka got 32. His sentence was the longest. Igor Sabljak was lucky. When he proved that he was a Croat, he was released. He was arrested because his wife was in Sremska Mitrovica. That's why they thought that he was a Serb. Unfortunately, he had the worst destiny. The third day after his arrest, his father hanged himself - he was also a doctor - and his mother ended up in the hospital, in the Intensive Care Unit, as a patient with a heart condition. The charges against us changed every so often and we lodged a complaint. The first one was for genocide. Then another charge was for leaving the military forces, even though we didn't have that kind of obligation because we had our job obligation. Then we were charged with abandoning our work obligation, when we filed complaints, that they did that, avoiding military obligation, for we did not have it at all. As for our other complaints, they put all the charges for the genocide, they left the complaints for the co-operation with the enemy. It was the charge for taking us before the Court."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Madam, Ms. Zaimovic, these were no longer paramilitary formations. This was a state structure. People were being sentenced to 28 months in prison. The young Kafka was sentenced to 32 months. Kafka's father is or was the old Kafka, a renowned doctor in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, and he died before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You see this poor man, Dr. Sabljak, was fortunate because he was a Croat, but his father committed suicide, hanged himself, and his mother had a heart attack. Did you know that the state was treating doctors this way in the middle of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about that. Marko Vukovic worked in the ER, whereas Dejan Kafka fled from pediatric surgery, and they probably arrested him then and tried him. What they are speaking about to you or, rather, on television, may be war propaganda that you conceived of together with them. I think that everyone should be heard so that they could tell the real truth. When they came to you, they probably had to say all sorts of things under duress so that you would trust them, and that it would be a type of war propaganda. That's what I think, at least. And I don't think it's fair from Vukovic or from Kafka, we took such good care of them. I think I can really say that we were so gentle to them that our own doctors were jealous because we took such care of them. We caressed them, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't mind caressing, myself. This looked like torture, though. How could they invent this kind of thing, renowned university professors, great surgeons? How could they invent things like this? D01003. Can we see that now so we can see what the result was --

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If these two or three men invented all of this --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Ms. Zaimovic, but what could have the young Kafka have done wrong? How could he be sentenced to 32 months in prison?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He left all the wounded, and it was his duty to stay by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Oh, Dr. Sosic; right, yes. Now let's see what the outcome was of all of this.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "This is just an example, illustrating that these men, these 400 doctors, were not fleeing because they thought that they were faring well, but because their lives were threatened. We as civilians couldn't do anything."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You heard Professor Sosic, who says, 400. I have a list of 250 doctors, but every day I am receiving information as people are watching these proceedings. 400 doctors left Sarajevo illegally, crossing the lines. Madam, was that the kind of caressing that you were involved in, that they had to flee from Sarajevo to the mountains as refugees? Were they fleeing from something good?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll answer that question. Dr. Sosic left because he had a weekend cottage in Pale and he had a place to go to together with his wife and two children, two sons. As for the other doctors, they all had their own reasons why they left. However, as a rule, once war had broken out, none of them should have left town. Had they stayed on, nothing would have happened to any one of them. On your territory where you were, every Muslim who stayed on was either killed or expelled. That was not the case in Sarajevo. So this war propaganda that I hear from Dr. Sosic, from his mouth, and I had endless respect for him, he was such a fine man, and his wife as well, now I'm truly disappointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Madam, you say that nothing would have happened to them had they stayed on. Did Professor Najdanovic stay on, and was he stabbed 14 times, and was he shot in the mouth? What happened to him?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please don't ask me about that. I just heard that he got killed. Now, what happened, actually, whether he stayed, or whether he fled, and whether he was caught, I really don't know what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sorry, but this sounds like what Mr. Izetbegovic said when Minister Ostojic was hit with an iron bar in the head. Izetbegovic said, Well, he probably got involved in a fight. This man was massacred.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dear me, Mr. Karadzic. The number of people you massacred, are you aware of that? You keep talking to me about some kind of massacres, and I want to tell you how many children you massacred in Sarajevo; 1.601 child.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We will still --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
