utterances.text: You have spent 20 [sic] hours getting nothing from this witness. You played this tape -- did I say "20 hours"? Twenty minutes. But the witness didn't come from any part of this tape. It's totally a waste of time. Discuss with your legal adviser how to properly use your variable time in the courtroom. Let's move on to another topic. Otherwise, let's conclude.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, but I think that the witness confirmed that she knew both persons involved, both doctors, both Vukovic and Sosic, Professor Sosic. And she confirmed that they worked there, and the reputation they had. I think this is recognised. Ms. Zaimovic doesn't want to admit that these things happened, but she did recognise these people. Can these videos be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the fact that she recognises the doctors is no basis for having the rest of the videotape admitted. They're quite similar just to witness statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see any reason to distinguish it with a witness statement, as you said. The Chamber will confer. Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I would just point out the witness did confirm more than just that these people existed; that she knew them. She confirmed elements of what they said, that they'd left, and that some of the events are, in fact, correct. I think that's enough of a threshold to distinguish this from some of the documents that you've excluded and should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But the evidence remains in the transcript regarding the recognition of certain persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, the video itself --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And as to the content of it. And then we haven't heard about the origin of this film yet, and who produced, and she didn't confirm any of the real content of it except for the recognition.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: She did confirm some of the elements of what was said by the person on the video, and I think you're making a very high bar to admission of evidence if you expect that everything in the document has to be confirmed or authenticated in that way. So at least I think there's a threshold that's been met, and perhaps it's difficult to pin-point exactly or calibrate exactly what that threshold is. But according to Judge Morrison's earlier statement, I think that we've at least had enough indication that there's a recognition of some of the elements in the statement for it to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. My point is whether this witness is the proper witness through whom this evidence can be introduced. The Chamber will confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will admit it by majority, me dissenting, and then it will be given the number. This consists of several clips, and the Chamber needs to confer again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. All of them which you were shown. I take it the numbers shown so far is: 1000 -- let's give the numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D1000 will be Exhibit D130; 1D1006 will be Exhibit D131; 1D1002 will be Exhibit D132; and 1D1003 will be Exhibit D133.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, thank you. Since both Prosecution and the witness have questioned certain matters - the Prosecution questioned the source and the witness said that Vukovic deserved 28 months in prison because he left his job - I would like to have a video-clip of 30 seconds played now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Madam, do you know this doctor on the screen?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Zijo Avdic?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we play this so that we would hear how much they worked, both him and Dr. Vukovic, incessantly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "It went on -- I don't know, lots of operations, minor ones and serious ones, and we finished at 5.00 in the morning. After the sentence, we filed a complaint and were taken back to prison. Of course, we're waiting for the judgement to be final."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please rewind this so that we hear that "My boss, Dr. Vukovic, also did this."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "And then this went on. I don't even know how many operations, minor ones, bigger ones. We finished at 5.00 in the morning. And it doesn't have to do only with me. It also has to do with my boss, Dr. Vukovic, who was working at 5.00 in the morning, and then it went on and on. I don't even know how long these operations went on, minor ones, major ones; 5.00 in the morning. "After the judgement, we were taken back to prison, and we filed a complaint, of course. And we were waiting for the judgement to become final, but by then we were exchanged."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So, Ms. Zaimovic, Dr. Zijo Avdic said that he was not leaving the operations room, he wasn't, and his boss, Dr. Vukovic, he did not leave at all. He worked as hard as possible, and he was sentenced to 28 months, and finally he was exchanged as a regular prisoner. He never filed a bullet, he had not sinned at all. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what to say. Dr. Vukovic worked at ER; very hard, at that. I don't know what happened, why he fled. Was it due to your propaganda? Was that why he had to leave? I don't have an answer to that question. As for his sentence, I really can't say anything about it. It's people who are involved in that kind of work that can say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He was not sent to prison. While he was waiting for the sentence of 28 months to start, he was exchanged like a regular prisoner or like a combatant that had been taken prisoner, but he, on the contrary, had been working day and night in your hospital. Thank you. Can we have this video-clip admitted into evidence, because it explains that these people were tried for nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is the 65 ter number of this? If Mr. Karadzic could confirm that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same, the number is the same. It's just a different part. This was telecast from Muslim Television, the state television from Bosnia-Herzegovina. 1002 is the number. It's within 1002.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the same reasons, I would object to this clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But, unfortunately, this is part of the exhibit we've already admitted. So on that basis, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to save time. However, since both the witness and the Prosecution asked about the source, they led to all of this. I had to play this clip as well. Can I ask for -- can I ask for a statement to be placed on the ELMO, please, a statement by yet another doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of Dr. Vladimir Simunovic?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is he a Croat?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what his ethnicity is, but I know that he was a neurosurgeon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And he came in through the same door like you did?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the same door that I did, until neurosurgery was moved to ER.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. I've just been handed a piece of paper. I've got no idea what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's what we got from the Prosecution. There's a number up there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I realise that, but, I mean, I don't know the 65 ter number, I don't know the purpose of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By now you should know the rule. You should inform the opposing party, the Prosecution, the documents you are going to use in advance, as well as its 65 ter number. Was it not listed in the list of the Defence exhibits to be used?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see -- well, it must have been a mistake. But we simply don't have enough resources, we don't have enough people. All of us are extremely busy, and it just happened this way. It's just one sheet of paper, but it's part of all of this evidence about everything that happened in the hospital where Ms. Zaimovic worked. I kindly ask that this be allowed now. But, believe me, we don't have the resources, we don't have enough people. They're working at full steam, but one of them soon will not even get any pay for what he's doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That can't be the reason, and by now you should be -- you should have been familiarised with the rule. Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's no translation, it's in B/C/S. I've got no idea --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's see how we can get on with it. Let's put it on the ELMO, and then let's see whether Ms. Zaimovic knows anything about it. What is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer I got was that Ms. Zaimovic knew Dr. Vladimir Simunovic, a very well-known younger doctor, an ethnic Croat, and he made a statement when he managed to escape from Sarajevo. He made a statement at Ilidza, and this is what he says: The second paragraph: "We have been informed that over the past few days, about 150 wounded soldiers from Azici were brought in."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's what you confirmed, that there were a lot of wounded soldiers in Azici, where your son was?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Doctors in hospital are being closely observed, and often they are being threatened with weapons, saying that they have to save some patients who had been brought in half dead. It is particularly difficult for doctors who are ethnic Serbs, and Croats as of late as well. We have also been informed that within the compound of the Kosevo Hospital, in the old laundry room and the restaurant above the ear department, there is the military police, consisting of about 200 men. They are commanded by Almir Husic, and he's using the pseudonym 'Kinez.' Near the Civil Engineering Faculty, there are some artillery weapons that are often firing, and in the tunnel of Ciglane, two armoured vehicles can be seen." And then down towards the bottom, it says: "Out of the doctors who are ethnic Muslim who are too extreme, the following should be mentioned: Dr. Faruk Kulenovic, Dr. Mufid Lazovic, Dr. Faris Gavrankapetanovic, Dr. Goran Dzinic, who are underrating Serbs in any way, and they are prepared to exchange for the ideas of Alija Izetbegovic their doctors' clothes for military uniforms." What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say that these are lies, and I'm sure that a doctor who wanted to leave town under the pressure exerted by your machinery said all of this so that you would let him leave Bosnia. This is such a lie. I wish I could see him myself and tell him that to the face. This is a pure lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That means, Ms. Zaimovic, that in Kosevo, where I had spent 50 years, only nurses tell the truth and the doctors lie as a rule; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you have just said is a lie. Please do not answer questions. I was not speaking about everybody. What Dr. Simunovic said under pressure, I'm sure it was under pressure, and the pressure was put on him in order for him to be able to leave. That's how your machinery worked, and that's why he put all Bosnian doctors to shame. And they worked day and night saving everybody, not even looking at their names, who they were. They treated everybody as if they were their own children. Please do not say those words.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me just remind you, Madam. He had already left Sarajevo, he had already left Sarajevo, and he was telling why he left, and he was telling what was going on in your city, under your authorities, in your hospital, and you don't know anything about that. All the doctors lie. Four-hundred doctors ran away, and you say that it was without any reason at all or under my pressure. How should I have done -- exerted any pressure in the Muslim part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was your pressure. They left because they wanted to save their families. Most of them left in order to save their families, and most left under your pressure, because you wanted them to leave. You wanted to have a better opportunity to shell Sarajevo and kill people. That was your goal. You always appealed to them, and they finally decided to save their families. And now what I've just read is nothing but a blatant lie. I would like to look at this doctor in the eye and ask him about this, and I will do it if I ever come across him walking through Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that all those people left their apartments and all of their property in Sarajevo, and you're still saying that it was because of me? Croats, Jews, everybody left their jobs, salaries, apartments, painters? This Simunovic was a collector of paintings. We all know that. So you're saying that they left all of that because of me?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What are material things? Material things are nothing. During the war, the only thing that mattered was life. You destroyed everything. You expelled thousands upon thousands of people. You confiscated everything they had. Your warriors took gold from our women. You killed anybody, anywhere. And what you are saying now, let me tell you, that people left Sarajevo and they left their apartments behind. What happened to them, I don't know, but I suppose that people sheltered refugees in those apartments. And what you are saying, Mr. Karadzic, now, you should be ashamed when you compare us in Sarajevo, that you pounded all the time, your people who slaughtered, killed, children, women, expelled poor old people from their homes. How can you even sleep after all that? I look you in the eye, I have turned towards you. Look at me. Can you go to sleep without dreaming about Croat and Serbian mothers who had loved their children? Can you do that? I'm talking to you as a mother, as a woman who doesn't know what arms are, who didn't know what a war was, but now knows what killing is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please bear in mind what Judge Baird has advised you, Ms. Zaimovic. Please try to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just one more question, and then I will say goodbye to you. Madam, you are saying that 15 professors lied, 400 doctors left everything they had in Sarajevo because they loved me and my political ideas, and you're the only person telling the truth. I would like to thank you for coming here. Say hello to my friend Islam and your son, whom I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have told only the truth from my soul, and I believe that it will be proven before this Trial Chamber. I apologise to the Trial Chamber for having said things that were not really within the protocol of this institution. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask whether this document can be admitted, because the lady said that she knew Dr. Simunovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, she said nothing about the statement. It will not be admitted. Ms. Sutherland, do you have redirect?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Zaimovic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you very much for your coming once again to the Tribunal, all the way from your place, to give it. And I hope you will have a safe trip back and stay well. Now you are free to go. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I seek your advice as to how we could identify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You may go now, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have mentioned that, together with the Prosecution, we could try and establish the position of Osmice in the map that the witness looked at and could not make that identification, because she was not able to identify Osmice in the map. But she knows where Osmice is. How can we try and identify that place in the map? That would be of some assistance to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Discuss it with Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: The short answer is probably that the Prosecutor won't disagree with the distance between two places on the map, which has a scale attached to it, and it can become an agreed document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, let's bring in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I be excused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The process of moving from witness to witness, and leading attorney to leading attorney, involves logging on and logging off, and that will take a few minutes. I leave it to the Court, if it wants to remain sitting or take a five-minute break, but we'll be logging off of one system and logging on to another. It will just take a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If we have a 25 minutes' break, then we can go through until 7.00, it will be about one and three-quarters of an hour. It may be too long, given the length of the tape. So we'll have a -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. There is going to be some dispute about the 65 ter documents. I don't know if we can maybe discuss that with Mr. Tieger and myself and the Chamber while the other attorneys are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: There's a whole host of documents that the Prosecution has identified as associated exhibits with the 92 ter package. And applying the Chamber's rule that the witness has to have adopted some portion of the contents of those documents or have knowledge of it, I find about 30 documents that don't seem to meet that criteria. And so I have a list of those documents which at this time we don't feel should be admitted. I can give you some examples or I can give you the whole list. Unfortunately, I didn't prepare anything in writing because I was reading these -- going through this shortly after you made your ruling. When I came this morning, I was not expecting to be objecting to these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There are some of those documents that will be shown to the witness during the course of his direct examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. But I must say that in light of scheduling issues that my colleague Mr. Tieger addressed you on earlier today, we have abbreviated or shortened the number that would otherwise be shown to the witness, given that they're already fully dealt with and integrated into his amalgamated statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that, could you put those numbers in writing, as well as brief reasons, so that we can deal with it the first thing tomorrow morning, after having heard his direct examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That would be helpful. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, at a minimum, Your Honour, I'd say that the associated exhibits in connection with this witness would fall into the same category as the previous witnesses. That's how this witness was prepared, and that's how the examination was dealt with, that's how the documents were tendered. If there's to be any departure from that, I think it would have to be following some express guidance from the Court, and I don't think this witness would fall within that category. I think that this is -- we should clearly proceed with this witness, as we have with the previous, and the determination of the associated exhibits should be made on the same basis; that is, whether they reflected -- whether they constituted an aspect of his previous examination. And I think that would be the only fair way to proceed, particularly, as Mr. Edgerton noted, since we reduced the length of the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now I understand the complaint of Judge Lattanzi. I waited for the French translation to be concluded. There's criteria or requirements for those documents to be admitted pursuant to 92 ter, or these things having, in my opinion, clarified -- have been made clear through our past decisions, and then the Chamber will consider Mr. Robinson's arguments in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Welcome, Mr. Harland. If you could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And my apologies for the brief delay, for the technical reasons, and it's been some time since I've appeared in Chambers. I had to find my way, somewhat. Now, that having been found, perhaps I can begin.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, could you please state first your name for the trial record, your full name?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: I'm David John Harland.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you've provided a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor regarding your experiences in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1998, testified before a Chamber of this Tribunal in the Slobodan Milosevic case in 2003, and again in the Dragomir Milosevic case in 2007; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: I think so. I'm not sure about the date of the original statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you visit the OTP, the Office of the Prosecutor, again in 2009 and prepare a statement consolidating the previously-recorded evidence we've just referred to, and referencing and commenting on a range of associated documents?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, prior to coming to court to testify today, have you had an opportunity to review that statement?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, on review of that document, is it correct that you had a number of clarifications and corrections you wished to make?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes, small ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you record those changes in a further written document?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if examined on all the same matters that led to the original statement and the testimonies you've given on two previous occasions that were consolidated into this statement, and asked the same questions, would you provide the same information to the Court?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: I hope so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, that having been said, could I tender then for admission, please, 65 ter 90011, which is Mr. Harland's consolidated statement, and 65 ter 22799 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, they will be admitted as ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 9011 will be Exhibit P820, and 65 ter 22799 will be Exhibit P821.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now with Your Honour's permission, then, if I may, I'd like to read a short summary of the written evidence of Mr. Harland. Mr. Harland worked for the United Nations in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in various capacities, from 1993 through to 1999. From May 1993 to January 1995, he was a civil affairs officer with UNPROFOR BH Command. From January to August 1995, he served as the head of Civil Affairs for Sector Sarajevo. In August 1995, he was deployed back to BH Command, where he worked as the political adviser to the UNPROFOR BH commander, General Rupert Smith. After the conflict ended, Mr. Harland remained for three years, serving as head of Civil Affairs for the United Nations Mission in Bosnia and Herzegovina, otherwise known as UNMIBH. He later returned to research and write a report on the fall of Srebrenica, on behalf of the Secretary-General. From 1993 to 1995, Mr. Harland frequently participated in meetings with leaders of the warring factions, including the Bosnian Serb leadership, and, in particular, the accused. During this period, Mr. Harland was also the principal political drafter for UNPROFOR and, as such, was responsible for authoring contemporaneous reports, including "Weekly Political Assessments," "Sector Sarajevo Weekly Sitreps," agreements, and other correspondence. Mr. Harland recalls arriving in Sarajevo in May 1993 and finding an eerily empty city. Anti-sniping barricades had been hastily erected, and people would leave their homes only for short periods to collect food or water. All areas of the city showed damage from shelling or gun-fire. Mr. Harland observed and was aware of shelling of the city of Sarajevo by Serb forces. While some shelling was used to repel Bosnian government offensives, often the shelling he observed was either disproportionate retaliation or, to quote, "background terror shelling," being shelling that had no identifiable military tactical purpose, but seemed intended to keep the civilian population of Sarajevo locked down and fearful. Mr. Harland also observed and was made aware of sniping of civilians by Serb forces. On two occasions, he personally witnessed a civilian fatally wounded immediately after being targeted by a sniper. Mr. Harland concluded that through this type of shelling, sniping, and by restriction placed on utilities and freedom of movement, Dr. Karadzic and the Bosnian Serb leadership were able to put pressure on Sarajevo, and would modulate this pressure for political ends. Mr. Harland describes this modulation as like turning "a spigot of terror." The shelling and sniping of civilians by Serb forces was frequently raised at meetings with the accused as well as other members of the Bosnian Serb leadership. The accused represented in meetings that he would or sometimes had issued orders to Serb forces to stop shelling and sniping. The cessation of sniping after the signing of the Anti-Sniping Agreement in August 1994 suggested to Mr. Harland that sniping activity was centrally controlled. Mr. Harland was in Sarajevo when the first Markale Market incident occurred in February 1994. He states that circumstantial evidence showed that the Serbs were responsible. He also states that the suggestion by the Bosnian Serb leadership at the time, that it was a hoax perpetrated by the Muslims using mannequin dummies or body parts flown in from the United States, was "outlandish, not to say a little deranged." Mr. Harland witnessed a deterioration of the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1995. Shelling and sniping in Sarajevo increased in May and June 1995, and Karadzic imposed severe restrictions on utilities and humanitarian access into the city. Bosnian Serb forces employed large and powerful improvised rockets against the city. The use of this type of weapon was directly protested by UNPROFOR to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps commander, Dragomir Milosevic. Mr. Harland was also in Sarajevo when the second Markale Market incident occurred in August 1995. He testifies that UNPROFOR's experts immediately concluded that the mortar bomb came from Bosnian Serb positions in the area of Lukavica. Comments by General Smith at the time, that there was some doubt as to the origin of fire, were made only to ensure that the Serbs were not alerted to the fact that he had requested NATO to begin air-strikes against Serb positions, and thus to allow for the safe extraction of peacekeepers from Bosnian-Serb-held territory, without which the air campaign could not have gone ahead. That concludes the summary, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Harland, if I may, I'd like to ask you a number of questions drawing upon and highlighting some aspects of the evidence recorded in your statement of 2009. First, you've had a longstanding career with the United Nations by this date; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How long have you been employed with the organisation?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Continuously since 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what's your present title?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: I'm the director of United Nations peacekeeping operations for Europe and Latin America.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could go back to your statement and your time in Sarajevo and in UNPROFOR. In paragraph 13 of this document, you described your functions in your role as civil affairs officer within BH Command as including: negotiations, analysis, reporting, and advising on political strategy. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, did these remain components of your work throughout your service for UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes, though the interlocutors changed a bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In what regard did they change?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Well, UNPROFOR, I mean, like all large organisations, had headquarters at different levels. It had a headquarters in Zagreb that covered the whole of the former Yugoslavia. It had a -- two levels of headquarters in Sarajevo; one so-called BH Command, which was the headquarters that covered all activities, operations of UNPROFOR throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I worked for most of my time at that headquarters. At the other end of the city, in the same city, was their headquarters for the smaller Sector Sarajevo, which was just one of three sectors within the Bosnia-Herzegovina command, and for a period I worked at that subordinate Sector Sarajevo headquarters as its civilian head. When I was at the BH Command level, normally I would be there in assistance to my superiors who were meeting with President Izetbegovic, with Dr. Karadzic, and characters at that level. When I was in Sector Sarajevo, I was generally meeting on my own behalf with the mayors or the corps commanders on either side.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, also in terms of your duties, at paragraph 17 of this statement from 2009, you noted you were also the principal political drafter for UNPROFOR; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And was this -- this component of your function, did that continue throughout your service with UNPROFOR as well?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what did it comprise, that component of your function?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Well, the UNPROFOR made regular reports to its headquarters in Zagreb and New York; on a weekly basis, normally. And I used a political assessment, and I normally wrote it, at least for most of the war. I think I was the longest serving UN official in Bosnia during the war, so for most of the war I wrote the weekly assessment. But then there were reports of meetings or incidents. So when there would be a meeting involving UNPROFOR with President Izetbegovic or Dr. Karadzic or General Mladic or General Delic, I would normally be present, and I would normally make a report of the meeting and usually draft a comment or an analysis of it. And so there was both the regular reporting and the reporting of meetings. There were also -- if there were incidents of special note, I would -- like you mentioned the Markale, one incident, that it might require a special cable or note, then normally I would draft it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In addition to the individuals that you've just named, President Izetbegovic, Dr. Karadzic, General Mladic, or General Delic, did you have other sources of information that you would rely on to prepare these reports and other documents?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes, a lot of them. I don't know how far you want me to go, but, I mean, first of all, we maintained an active set of contacts in Sarajevo and in Pale. So in Sarajevo, I would see almost every day representatives of the Bosnian government at the ministerial level. The point of entry was usually -- for most of the conflict was Hasan Muratovic. But on the Bosnian Serb side, we also kept in regular touch with Professor Koljevic, the vice-president; Mr. Krajisnik, the speaker of the Assembly. We also had a range of contacts in the military, General Mladic, Milovanovic, and Generals Galic and Milosevic, as well as their counterparts on the Bosnian side. I'm working my way down slowly, and I could go on for a very long time. But suffice it to say that this eventually reaches the soldiers we would meet at check-points and people we would encounter on the street or in hospitals or in morgues. It was generally the job of Civil Affairs to keep a very active network of interlocutors on all sides to be able to provide multiple streams of information into our analysis.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, moving on to another subject, perhaps you could tell us, did the topography of Sarajevo affect the nature of the conflict around the city?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Oh, yes, enormously. I mean, Sarajevo, as the Court's probably heard, lies in a narrow, steep valley. It runs from west to east for, I think, about 10 kilometres in a mountainous area in the middle of Bosnia. So because the floor of the valley is narrow and not terribly long, the population is highly concentrated. And wherever you live in the city, you have the perception of being, you know, at the bottom of a bowl of mountains. And for historical reasons that I think -- and geographical reasons that are well understood, but probably not so interesting to the Court, the Bosniak population in Sarajevo, as in almost all other areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina, tended to live on the -- in the urban areas, on the floors of these valleys. And at normal times, I suppose it didn't matter. But in the context of the war, it meant that the high ground throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina, but, you know, perhaps especially in Sarajevo, the high ground was dominated by the Serbs, with their weaponry, and the low ground was a relatively compact community of mainly Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Over the course of your service with UNPROFOR, did you see any pattern or any dynamic to the conflict around the city?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes. The confrontation line didn't change very much during the whole period that I was there. In fact, it changed very little. What changed substantially was the volume of fire over the confrontation line and the availability of the means of life for the civilian population. So, broadly speaking, there were seven or eight or nine levers of control that the Serbs could try to exert on the population; shelling, sniping, other small-arms fire, the passage of convoys of humanitarian aid from the United Nations, the availability of gas, water, and electricity, most of which had to flow into Bosnian government-controlled territory from Bosnian-Serb-controlled territory. So there was definitely a dynamic of the conflict that involved the increasing application of pressure, or what I sometimes call terror, by the Bosnian Serbs, and that is the sniping, and the shelling, and the restriction of water and gas, and the convoys and so on, and this would follow discernible patterns.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you see those patterns as being linked to anything?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Well, first we felt that they were -- we -- there was quite a lot of evidence that they were centrally controlled, that is, that the sniping and the shelling would normally increase at the same time that there would be increasing restrictions on the movement of humanitarian convoys, on the -- that there would be increasing restrictions on the gas, water, or electricity. So they were linked to each other, that is, in the sense that they normally got better or worse, whether military or civilian, in tandem, in concert. Also, the overall modulation definitely reflected the particular political context.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In what way?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: The most obvious way is that when there was an explicit threat of intervention against the Bosnian Serbs, that the pressure would go dramatically down, would be eased, until the immediate threat of military intervention had passed. When, on the other hand, there was little threat, then, generally, the application of that spigot of terror, as I called it, would go up.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you, for all of us, identify any manifestations of those -- or examples of these situations that you've described?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: I can, but I should say, in a way, it doesn't even need to be proved. I mean, the Bosnian Serb leadership would say so directly to us, that this was what was happening. But just to give an example, then: I arrived early in the summer or late in the spring of 1993, just as the Serbs were about to begin an offensive in the area of Igman and Bjelasnica, close to Sarajevo. That offensive, as usual with their military offensives, was successful. But as it drew to its conclusion, the Western countries made -- a group of them, NATO -- including the Secretary-General, NATO made some explicit threats or explicit references to the possibility or the need to use air-strikes against Bosnian Serbs around Sarajevo. At about this time, we would note -- so this is then middle or late July. We would notice a dramatic decline in the Serb shelling of the down-town area or the sniping of civilian population. Humanitarian aid would be allowed to flow again. Gas and water and electricity would become more generally available. And if one were to plot this on a graph over time, one would see this sharp dip in the pressure, the terror, being applied to the population of Sarajevo during my period after Igman, the Igman offensive, certainly after Markale 1 incident in February of 1994, and then again when there was another round of threats by NATO, and then again after Gorazde, and so on. So the pattern was highly discernible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Do you have something to say, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection. First of all, Ms. Carolyn was kind enough to talk to me, and we agreed that there would be nothing about feelings. Second of all, Mr. Harland has already made a judgement. He already mentions the word "terror." Could please somebody protect my interests? Otherwise, I will have to go on objecting. We have already agreed we would not be talking about feelings and other psychological elements, but, rather, just about facts. This is a judgement before a judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You'll have the opportunity to cross-examine the witness during your cross-examination. Let's proceed, Ms. Edgerton. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. Thank you, but perhaps I could use this to direct us to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, at page 70, line 21, of this transcript, and at another occasion later, you've used -- you've referred to the word "terror," and we noticed that you used that word in a number of contemporaneous UNPROFOR documents you authored, some of which are referred to in your statement, as well as in your statement itself. And perhaps I could ask that 65 ter 10678 be called up in this regard. No, that's correct, there's not. The document should be available in English only. Thank you very much. Mr. Harland, do you see an image of a document on the screen in front of you, the monitor in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you tell us what it is, please?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: It is a Sector-Sarajevo-level weekly situation report, so it is a review of the main events relevant to UNPROFOR's mandate in the area of Sarajevo from the 8th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you write this document?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if I could ask us all to move to e-court page 2 of this document, fifth paragraph down the page, that would be very helpful. Now, I'll just see if I have counted right. Yes, I think so. Could I direct your attention, Mr. Harland, to the paragraph that begins with the words: "Sniping and mortaring ...," and ask you to read to us these first two sentences.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: "Sniping and mortaring are still at a reasonably high level. This seems to have no particular military value but contributes to a general atmosphere of terror in the city. Almost no civilians now use the city's main east-west thoroughfare," so-called Sniper Alley, "so much so that snipers who used to work that area now seem to have relocated ."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, do you recall, even broadly speaking, the safety and security situation in the city of Sarajevo at around this time?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what was that situation?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: It was very bad, I mean. And when I used the word "terror," I didn't mean it in any emotional way. I simply tried to reflect the feeling of the population as a result of these various levers of pressure that I've described, the shelling and the sniping and the small arms and the lack of humanitarian assistance and so on. I would be happy to use a different word if there were one the Court thought was suitable.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if I may first, Your Honours, that having been heard, tender 65 ter 10678, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P822, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection as well. I have an objection as well, in terms of other people's feelings, the expression of other people's feelings. I don't think that's right. [In English] The feelings of the population --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are dealing with the admission of documents. And as to the content, you can have ample opportunity to cross-examine Mr. Harland during your cross-examination. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in your statement, at paragraphs 32 and 33, you describe three distinct forms of bombardment of Sarajevo by Serb forces, one being, and I quote "tactical use of heavy weapons," the second being, and I quote, "tit-for-tat," when Bosnian forces would fire some rounds onto Serb-held territory and there would be a strong response by the Serbs, and the third which you describe as "background terror," and that's a quote, shelling with no identifiable military purpose. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I ask, then, that we bring up the next document, 65 ter 09599, please, Weekly Political Assessment 39, dated 3 November 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you see the document on the screen before you, Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise the document?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you draft the document?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: So this is from an earlier period in my life from the one you mentioned last time, so this is when I was working at the BH Command, that is, the higher-level headquarters. And so this is the weekly political assessment, so it's the weekly report that is sent to Zagreb and New York, which seeks to describe and analyse the principal events relevant to UNPROFOR's mandate from the preceding week.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we move over to, please, e-court page 7 of this document. And if I could draw everyone's attention to the first paragraph at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Harland, would you be able to read that first paragraph for us into the record?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: This is like a trip to the optometrist: "The Serbs -- " Yes, the top -- the first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: First paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: "The Serbs have been militarily more active than usual recently. They have not been trying to take territory, but their artillery has been busy. Sarajevo and Gorazde have both been under heavy bombardment in the past week. In response to BH mortar fire, the Old Town of Sarajevo received almost 500 shells in a one-hour period on 27 October. The Old Town, which has the highest percentage of Muslims in any Sarajevo area, is densely populated."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I ask you, then, relating to the distinct forms of bombardment you described in your statement, which of the three types of shelling was this?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Well, if it was in response to mortar fire from the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, then -- from the Bosnian government army, then it was the second type in the way I categorised them. So, yeah, it was the retaliatory fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you describe the size of area of the Old Town to us, please, and give us an idea of the type of structures found in that part of the city?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Well, the heart of it is an area of a kilometre or so in radius around the Bascarsija market-place, and it's a maze of little streets that normally buildings of just one or two or sometimes three-storeys, with little tiled roofs. It's a densely-packed little picture of an Ottoman city.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Whenever it's convenient, we could have a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I just tender this document, that would perhaps be, following that, an appropriate moment for the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be admitted as ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P823, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will have a 25 minutes' break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's actually Edgerton, Your Honour, but we've never had the pleasure. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I apologise, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: None needed, Your Honour. If I may, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, if we could perhaps move now over to the subject of one of these levers of pressure, or another one of these levers of pressure you referred to just a little while ago in your testimony. I'd like to ask you about sniping. Was sniping of civilians in Bosnian-government-held territory by Bosnian Serb forces prevalent throughout your tour in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes, though it varied a lot from time to time, the rate of fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But it was a constant feature, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes. It almost disappeared during a short period in the autumn of 2004, I think, but --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Leading questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- but it was, in general, prevalent at some level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Leading questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He already answered. But, yes, given the nature of 92 ter evidence, we allowed, until objected to, to go on, leading questions. But could you bear that in mind in further questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, and my apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you make observations about its affect on the daily life of civilians?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what did you, yourself, see?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Well, the -- between the shelling and the sniping, the basic effect was to keep people off the streets. When you entered Sarajevo, you would not believe at all it was a city of 2- or 300.000 people. It was quiet, except for gun-fire. The streets were mostly empty. It's not until you went into the entranceways and into people's apartments that you noticed that the city was full. So that was the first thing. Specifically about sniping is that people, when they had to go out, avoided the places that were exposed to sniper fire; open intersections, any street that is perpendicular to the confrontation line, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you see local inhabitants taking measures to protect themselves from sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes, and that happened at all levels. So individuals put up blankets on ropes, or they covered windows, or they tipped over burnt-out cars. Also, the Bosnian government authorities erected barricades of cars and slabs of concrete to obscure the line of sight from Serbian-held positions. And I should say UNPROFOR also did this. UNPROFOR's preferred method was the placement of sea containers in blocks, like a child's Lego blocks, on a large scale to block the line of site from Serbian positions into the centre of the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Have you, yourself, ever seen any incidents of sniping of civilians within the city?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Well, I was shot at a couple of times while in the city, and I never saw anybody being hit by sniper fire. But I have certainly been, many times, at an intersection where -- exposed to the confrontation line, where suddenly there would be -- you know, several shots would ring out, and people would spring back behind the protection and cower there and wait or find another way to get past or to go home. And a couple of times I have -- twice, I arrived on the scene of a sniper attack just after someone had been hit.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In those couple of times, did you see the victims?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes. Once, not well, in 1993. I think it was a woman in, I think, the Hrasno area, at a distance I was. I was in my vehicle. The other time, I was walking down one of the main streets, the street that before the war was known as Djure Djakovica, now I think Alipasina, the street where our headquarter was located, and there was at least one shot around the corner, and I rushed around the corner to find a group of people wanting to surge forward to get to a teenage boy who was injured next to a bicycle, and -- but fearing, and there was more firing and they hung back. But I never was actually watching when somebody was hit by a sniper.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To move a little bit back to the beginning of your testimony, you spoke about the source of information you relied on in carrying out your function and preparing your assessments and recommendations, and you noted you took part in meetings with different leaders of the warring factions. And I could also note in your statement, at paragraphs 15 to 16, 19, to 47, to 266, you referred to those meetings. And now I'd like to ask you for a little further detail in that regard. Were you involved, during the course of your service with UNPROFOR, in meetings with Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And was that -- did those take place in any period in particular?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes. They all took place while I was one of the political officers -- one of the civil affairs officers at BH Command, so that means they took place between June of 1993 and the last days of 1994, or perhaps the first days of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: At those meetings, do you recall ever seeing or hearing Dr. Karadzic issue military directives or give orders?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, we do not agree. If you could answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recall him saying, We have taken certain decisions about certain military matters, and in the presence of General Mladic and General Milovanovic, but I cannot say I ever directly heard him order one of them to do something. But he certainly spoke from authority, and even though, in particular, General Mladic would sometimes voice some separate opinion, he would indicate that he would -- he would do what Dr. Karadzic had said.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in one regard I note I didn't ask you for something earlier. I see, at page 81, line 18, you've mentioned the name of General Milovanovic, and I omitted earlier to ask you who General Milovanovic was, as far as you understood.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Well, at least during the time I was there, he seemed to be the Chief of Staff of the Bosnian Serb Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, on these occasions you've just mentioned at which General Milovanovic would sometimes -- sorry, pardon me, at which General Mladic would sometimes voice some separate opinion, he would indicate that he would do what Dr. Karadzic said, could you pin-point that, perhaps, in time?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Well, the one that sticks in my memory is the one from the end of the Igman crisis, so it must be August of 1993, where we had a meeting in Pale and about whether or not Serb forces would withdraw from Mount Igman and Bjelasnica, and the precise circumstances and conditions under which they would withdraw. And there was some degree of contention on the Serb side. General Mladic and also Dr. Plavsic were expressing some concern, if I remember correctly, and making some arguments as to why it should not be done or should not be done in a certain way, and then Dr. Karadzic decided and said that it would be done and would be done in a particular way. And then, in fact, some of my colleagues went off with General Mladic to survey the ground and to make the precise arrangements.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned here, at page 82, line 14, the name of Dr. Plavsic. And who is Dr. Plavsic, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: She was vice-president of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in regard to the Igman crisis that you've referred to, could I ask that 65 ter 10410A be called up, please. Could you move to page 2 of the English language document that we see on the screen in front of us, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Harland, you see an image on the screen in front of you. Does this document refer to the meeting in August 1993 that you've just talked about at page 82 of the transcript?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Well, I don't have page 82 of the transcript in front of me, I don't think, but that's a description of the meeting I think we were talking about, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could just -- if I could just ask you: You wrote that document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes, but it has some terrible name misspelling. So, yes, it seems so.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could move to page 3 of this document, please. Actually, I'd like to direct us to the first paragraph at the very top of page 3, but I see it begins the page previously. And I apologise to the Court. I made every effort to get my page numbers correct. So could we go back to page 2, the paragraph at the bottom of the page, yes, where we see the words: "Karadzic appeared relaxed, confident, and co-operative."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you please read this paragraph that flows from page 2 to page 3 onto the record?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: "Karadzic appeared relaxed, confident and co-operative. He presented proposals on Serb withdrawal from Mount Igman on the --"

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And could we move to page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "-- establishment of safe routes in and out of Sarajevo and on co-operation for the restoration of utilities. He indicated that these Serb initiatives would encourage Izetbegovic to rejoin the talks and would remove any suggestion of the use of air-strikes."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is this an example of the modulation you've discussed in your statement and in your testimony earlier?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I ask this document be admitted, please, 10410A.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be admitted as ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P824, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we move next to 65 ter 11287, please. It's a one-page document, and there should be an English translation available. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, do you see the document -- I'm sorry, the magnification that I see of the English language document is a little bit too big and it cuts it off the screen.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: No, mine is the -- on the left is the English translation of an order in B/C/S which appears on the right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But now I can see all the paragraphs. Mr. Harland, this is an order that, in the English translation, reads "Command of SRK," and is dated 11 August 1993. And the name at the bottom of the document reads "Commander Brigadier-General Stanislav Galic." Do you know who Commander Brigadier-General Stanislav Galic was?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes. He was at this time, I think, the commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. I mean, that is the main Serb military unit around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you place this document in context of the meeting you've just discussed?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yeah. So this is an order indicating that the level of -- I'm looking for a neutral word -- the level of pressure on Sarajevo should be -- should be reduced, that they shouldn't be firing on Sarajevo, and that this is a -- this is a response to the -- to the --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this is an expert opinion rather than testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I don't -- we don't agree. He can testify as far as he --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's an order clearly reducing the level of pressure on Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Reducing the level of pressure in response to anything in particular, as far as you can see?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Well, yes. It even says that the -- it states, at the beginning of the English text, that the United States and others are seeking to bomb Serb positions, and that in order to avoid that, they will greatly reduce the pressure on Sarajevo. I mean, they will, among other things, not open fire on Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is this another example of the modulation you've discussed in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's a leading question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Because doesn't that exclude the alternative answer, we do not agree it is a leading question. You can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is an example, a clear example, of them modulating the level of pressure or terror on Sarajevo in accordance with their political interests and conveniences.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could I ask that this document -- I'd like to tender this document as the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think this document would not be admissible under the rules, as I understand them, that the Trial Chamber is operating under, because the witness had no -- has no knowledge, other than saying that this document, which he apparently didn't have any knowledge of at the time, is consistent with his general knowledge of the situation. So it doesn't -- he's not adopting the document or being able to speak to it, other than being like a newspaper article or some other document that he could say confirms his view. But it doesn't have any significance other than that, so I don't believe it's admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You will address the admission issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour, because I had the benefit of hearing the Court's previous guidance. I believe it falls -- it's difficult to say what falls squarely within the Court's guidance, but it certainly falls well within the parameters of admissibility identified by the Court previously, looking for the various factors involved, including a number of the previous factors we mentioned; where they intersect, the official nature of the document, the elucidation by the witness, the nexus to the events that he described. Placing this particular document in context, it's difficult to see how -- I mean, it's easy to see how this illuminates the issues for the benefit of the Chamber. This is a document which could obviously come in in a variety of ways, including the fact that it's an official document. But in this particular context, the witness was asked about the factors contained within this document, related them to the events that he participated in, and illuminated its significance in a meaningful way for the Court. It's exactly the kind of inquiry that should be made to witnesses and exactly the kind of both context and significance that persons involved in events on the ground can provide to the Court when they are presented with contemporaneous documents. So I would ask that it -- definitely ask that this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? May I say something before your decision? This document is not being sent to me. It is being sent to subordinates. What can that have to do with my own thinking or my own conduct at a particular meeting? I think that everything that Mr. Tieger said is not in line with the existing decision made by the Trial Chamber. What is particularly important is the fact that this document of General Galic's is not sent to me, and that's why I don't think this would be right. On the other hand, the distinguished Mr. Harland, who speaks in a very baroque manner and is highly talented, from a literary point of view, he is speaking of people's feelings, and in this case General Galic's feelings and thoughts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber finds this document relevant or of probative value and authentic. In particular, authenticity has not been challenged. And the Chamber is of the view that the witness confirmed part of the content of this document to the effect that it is consistent with his observation he formed at the time. So according to the rule, the objection is overruled, and we admit this document. It will be admitted as ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P825, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: P825. And, Mr. Karadzic, as to your challenge, whether or not this document was sent to you, is not an issue at the time of admissibility. Rather, it is a matter of weight to be assessed at a later stage, to be done by the Chamber. Mr. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Harland, just to go briefly back to the subject of these meetings that we were discussing with members of the Bosnian Serb leadership, including Dr. Karadzic, during these meetings did you hear incidents of shelling or sniping protested to Dr. Karadzic or other members of the Bosnian Serb political or military leadership?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you comment generally on any responses you might have heard?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Well, in the case of Dr. Karadzic, normally he would deny that there was a problem, or say that he would look into the problem, or say that he had already issued orders that firing should stop.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In that note, are you aware -- do you have any knowledge, then, as to the effectiveness of these protests?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Well, in general, they would have very little effect, similarly with the written protests, the letters we would send, except at these times of explicit military threat from NATO forces against Serbs, in which case sometimes they might be responded to quite positively and the decisions might be implemented.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you ever hear incidents -- to go to the more particular, perhaps, did you ever hear of these incidents protested to General Mladic in the course of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And was there any reaction? And if so, what?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Well, General Mladic reacted in an entirely different way from Dr. Karadzic. Of course, he's a much more confrontational type of character. Dr. Karadzic would often link one problem to another, generally ensuring that the problem could never be resolved. For example, one I happen to remember - I don't know why - is there was a problem with the water supply in Sarajevo, as usual, and we would raise it during a certain period. And Dr. Karadzic would link it to the issue of the water supply in the place he called Srbobran [phoen], which turned out, after some confusion on our side, to be Donji Vakuf. Whereas General Mladic would generally be much more direct and combative in his rejections of our protests.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move forward or move on to another topic that you've spoke about in your testimony and statement, and that's the events of 5 February 1994. But perhaps before we talk about the events of that day in detail, could I ask you to provide us with some -- or do you recall the safety and security situation in Sarajevo in late January/early February 1994?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: It was bad. That was a period in which there was no explicit threat by NATO or anybody else of use of force against Serbs. That was a period after the Bosnian government had rejected the Owen-Stoltenberg Peace Plan a couple of months earlier. So there was generally very little reason on any side to restrain military activity, and so it was a period in Sarajevo that was characterised by rather a high level of shelling and small-arms fire and sniping, as well as quite tight controls on water, gas, electricity, and convoys, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And over the course of your work, did you become familiar -- or are you familiar with the events surrounding the shelling of 5 February 1994 that's now widely referred to as "Markale 1"?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What were your sources of information regarding the incident?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: There were a series of investigations into the incident that were formally undertaken by our UNMOs, that is, our United Nations Military Observers, by the French battalion responsible for the area, and by the UNPROFOR force engineers. In addition, I sent immediately to the scene of the incident one local colleague, who was a medical doctor, who -- so we were -- I was at the -- I was at Sarajevo Airport when news came of the incident, there with Mr. Krajisnik and Professor Koljevic, I think, and then Dr. Silajdzic and Dr. Muratovic, and news came that there had been this. And General -- we decided amongst ourselves at UNPROFOR that General Rose and our local colleague, Dr. Mocibob, would go immediately to the scene, whereas I would return to the headquarters and make contact. So I was aware of the investigation, and then I -- which I read and discussed with the authors, and then I de-briefed the investigators as well as General Rose and Dr. Mocibob.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I ask, please, that 65 ter 09625 be called up.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for that document to appear on the screen, perhaps I could ask you: Did you go to the scene, yourself?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the scene?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And how so?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Well, it's the main market-place in that part of Sarajevo. In many ways, it's Sarajevo's principal market-place.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if I could ask you to look at the document on the monitor in front of you entitled "Weekly BiH Political Assessment 53." Could I ask you if you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you draft that document?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I then ask if we can turn to e-court page 5, second full paragraph on page 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, the paragraph begins with the word: "Later." I note in this paragraph, you report in this document on a statement by Assembly President Krajisnik, and I'll read from the document: "In a similar vein, Assembly President Krajisnik claimed that many of the dead bodies seen on TV were not real people at all, but just mannequin dummies dressed up to look like blast victims." Now, based on the information you received, do you give any credence to this whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: No. That was completely bizarre and, if I may say so, to me illustrated just how distant to reality some of the power leadership were.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And why do you not give any credence to it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Well, among other things, I dispatched from my own staff a colleague who's a medical doctor, who's very well qualified to say what is the difference between a dead body and a mannequin. And these were definitely dead people, and there were definitely many taken to hospital, the survivors. Yes -- no, there was simply no question, and the whole suggestion is outlandish.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask this document please be admitted as the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P826.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Moving on, but still in relation to the same incident, and it's referred to, in part, in paragraphs 82 to 86 of your statement, could I ask for 65 ter 09632 to be called up on the screen, please, an UNPROFOR Weekly BiH Political Assessment 54, dated 17 February 1994. And there it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you write it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could move now over to e-court page 6 of this document, the very first paragraph of page 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in that very first paragraph, you've noted the following: "The Serb policy was summed up by Assembly President Krajisnik, who stated that, 'We will do everything to avoid air-strikes, except capitulate.'" Do you have any comment with regard to this notation that you made at the time and this statement?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Well, nothing except that it is an extremely explicit and specific example of the way in which the Serbs would suddenly reduce the level of shelling and sniping and restrictions of electricity and gas and so on, in response to perceived external threats. And here, they state it themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document please be made the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P827, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
