utterances.text: Moving on in time to the end of August 1995 and the incident frequently referred to as "Markale 2," could I ask you whether you're familiar with the incident or became familiar with the incident in the course of your work?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you attend the scene?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: I did pass the scene. I did go down to the scene some hours after. Markale 2, I think, happened in the late morning. In the evening, I passed by the scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And did you also -- or are you also aware of reports prepared and investigations conducted relating to the incident?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes, very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And how did you become aware?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: I was in the room when General Smith ordered an immediate investigation, and I was present in the hours and day or two that followed when those who prepared those reports were summoned and asked to give their analysis of what had happened and where the firing had come from.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I then ask for 65 ter 01692 to be called up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you see a document on the screen in front of you, Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes, a note to General Smith from the intelligence cell.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And how so?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: I was -- I was present when that document was presented to General Smith in the presence of the chief of the G2 cell, the intelligence cell, Colonel Powers, and I was present when these handwritten annotations or amendments were made to the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I note that this document refers to not one, but five mortar rounds having impacted; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, was one of those rounds the killing round?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To your knowledge, and based on your presence when this document was presented to General Smith and others, was there any doubt in BH Command as to the origin of fire of these five shells?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And did UNPROFOR issue any statements as to the origin of fire of these shells?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: The commander, General Smith, made a statement, saying that it was -- I forget the words, but saying that it was perhaps still not clear where -- what was the origin of fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And do you know, then, why such a statement might have issued when there was no doubt, to your knowledge, as to the origin of fire?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And why was that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: It takes a minute or two, if that's okay. There, General Smith had a plan to end the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, or at least a series of initiatives that would contribute to the end of the war, and central to those initiatives was the need to direct NATO air-strikes against the Bosnian Serbs on a massive scale. In order for him to be able to initiate those air-strikes, he had to resolve two problems. One problem, we called them the Mogadishu problem, which is probably less relevant to this Court, and to his statement about these mortars. The second problem is the hostage problem, which is that he could not trigger the large-scale -- the massive-scale use of NATO air power against the Bosnian Serbs unless he was sure that all UN personnel, particularly UN personnel of NATO nationalities, were off Bosnian Serb territory, because if they were on Bosnian Serb territory, they would be very vulnerable to being taken hostage. And they had -- the Serbs had shown, in May, I think it was, that if they were able to take hostages, they could use them as human shields, and that would stop NATO from escalating its air-strikes. So General Smith had been working for several weeks, very quietly and discreetly, to take as many UNPROFOR personnel as possible, particularly all those from NATO nations, off Bosnian-Serb-held territory. Now, nobody could predict, when this Markale atrocity happened, that this would be the incident that would trigger these air attacks, and very unfortunately for UNPROFOR, exactly on that day there was a small unit of very vulnerable British troops, that is, UNPROFOR troops of NATO nationality, stuck on Bosnian-Serb-controlled territory. I think it was a unit that was leaving the Bosnian government pocket of Gorazde -- enclave of Gorazde and going home, or rotating for leave, perhaps, and they were, I think, in a little village called Dobrun. So General Smith desperately needed a few hours of time. He needed to buy a few hours so that he could quickly get these British troops out of the way of the Serbs, so they couldn't be taken as human shields, so he needed a few hours in which the Serbs didn't realise what was happening while he prepared to launch the air-strikes. So we had a discussion about what to do, and it was decided that the best way to ensure that the Serbs did not quickly try to grab these people as hostages would be for us to make a very bland statement, a statement implying that we didn't know who had fired the shell, and certainly wouldn't imply that we were doing what was being done, which -- by UNPROFOR, which is preparing very large-scale air-strikes in an effort to end the war. So it was decided that such a statement would be made, and it was made. And I believe it may have contributed to an enduring myth as to who fired that mortar bomb.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document that remains on the screen, please, 65 ter 01692, if that could please be admitted as the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit P828.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, subject to resolution of the remaining associated documents that are referred to, expounded upon, and otherwise mentioned in Dr. Harland's statement, and which are contained in our notification of 29 April this year, that would conclude my examination-in-chief. I would, at this point, move these documents, which I think total some 92 in number, into evidence, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We have five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Judge Morrison has one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Harland, before Dr. Karadzic commences: You mentioned the Mogadishu factor, as it was a sort of almost, in a plea of confessional avoidance. I presume that what you meant by that would be the reluctance of certain powers to be involved as a result of what was widely acknowledged to have happened to US troops in Mogadishu.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a way. The very specific issue was that General Smith was concerned, as General Rose, his predecessor, had been, that if he, as the UNPROFOR commander, ordered massive air-strikes against the Serbs, that the Serbs would, because they controlled the artillery in the mountains around Sarajevo, be able to retaliate very directly against the UNPROFOR and UNHCR bases and facilities on the floor of the valley, that we would be vulnerable, just as the Bosnian government and the Sarajevo population had been vulnerable. And that if there was a massive retaliation by the Serbs, that the countries which owned the aircraft, the United States and other countries, might lose their nerve, in the face of casualties, and might withdraw, as had happened in Mogadishu. So General Smith determined that he would need a military plan before UNPROFOR called in NATO air-strikes on a massive scale. He would need to bring in large artillery units, which he placed on Mount Igman, and he would need to deploy them so that simultaneously with the order to launch air-strikes, he would be able to bombard the Serb artillery to suppress the Serbian battery fire. So this complicated sequence of events we called the Mogadishu problem. UNPROFOR was able to resolve the Mogadishu problem and the hostage problem, and the air-strikes were able to go ahead and help end the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll rise for today, but tomorrow morning I would appreciate if Mr. Robinson will have put into writing, just in a bullet point, the list of number of exhibits and --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correction, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- the crux of your objections so that we can deal with it for the first thing tomorrow morning. And Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 38, line 23, there is something that I didn't say, and it was recorded. However, it looks like a swear word. You can maybe check it on the audio. It seems that -- it arises from the transcript I said, "Madam damn," and I never said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be taken care of. Thank you. Tomorrow, we'll sit in the morning. Is it correct? Yes. Tomorrow morning, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 7th day of May, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.57 p.m.,
